common_name: Republic of Texas Lime (Cold-Hardy Thornless Lime)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring after frost danger passes in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Republic of Texas is grown widely as a large patio container plant in zone 8b–9 so it can be moved under cover on the coldest nights, and planted in the ground only in zone 9b–11 or the most protected zone 9a microclimates.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, or grow in a large container that can be sheltered during hard freezes; Republic of Texas is a nearly thornless lime of uncertain hybrid parentage that has become a favorite dooryard and patio citrus across the Gulf South because it is noticeably more cold-tolerant and heat-tolerant than true Key lime, while still delivering a strongly aromatic, classic lime flavor. Trees are vigorous, heavy-bearing, and begin fruiting young, producing abundant small to medium, thin-skinned, seedy fruit that ripens from pale green to yellow — harvest while still green for the brightest acidity, since fully yellow fruit turns sweeter and less lime-like. It is self-fertile and does not need a pollinizer. In zone 9a, site trees against a south-facing wall for extra winter protection and wrap or cover young trees during freeze events; established in-ground trees recover from light freeze damage by resprouting from the trunk. Fertilize with a citrus-specific blend three times during the growing season and keep the root zone mulched but not piled against the trunk.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Citrus for Texas Home Landscapes
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Louisiana Citrus Guide
Dave Wilson Nursery / retail citrus nursery variety notes

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root plants in late winter to spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Grenada is self-fruitful and productive on a single plant, and its cold hardiness makes it reliable well up into zone 7.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil of almost any pH in full sun; Grenada is a long-cultivated heirloom pomegranate variety passed down through Central Texas homesteads and nurseries, valued for combining good cold hardiness with the classic sweet-tart flavor and deep-red arils of a fully flavored pomegranate, unlike some ultra-hardy selections bred mainly for toughness over taste. Plants bear as a multi-stemmed large shrub or can be trained to a small single-trunk tree, produce showy orange-red trumpet flowers over a long season that attract hummingbirds, and are extremely drought-tolerant once established, needing little supplemental water beyond the first year or two. Fruit ripens in September and October, signaled by a hollow sound when the fruit is tapped and skin that has taken on full color; harvest promptly once ripe, since fruit left too long on the plant is prone to splitting after rain. Prune out root suckers to maintain a tidy shape and remove crossing interior branches each winter to keep the canopy open for good fruit coloring and air circulation.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Pomegranates for Texas
Texas Superstar / regional heirloom fruit nursery variety notes

planting.note: Plant during winter dormancy in very acidic, well-drained soil; Austin requires about 400–500 chill hours and needs a cross-pollinating companion such as Climax or Brightwell for good fruit set, since it is not self-fruitful.

directions: Amend soil to a strongly acidic pH 4.5–5.0 with peat moss or sulfur before planting; Austin is a rabbiteye blueberry released by the University of Georgia breeding program, selected as an early-to-midseason ripening variety that fills the harvest window alongside Climax, extending the picking season before the midseason varieties come on. Berries are medium-large, light blue, and firm with good flavor, borne on vigorous, upright, productive bushes that establish quickly. Like all rabbiteye blueberries, Austin is not self-fruitful and should be planted with at least one other compatible variety within about 50 feet for cross-pollination and full crops. Remove flower buds the first year or two after planting to direct the plant's energy into root and cane development rather than fruit; full production typically begins by year four. Mulch generously with pine bark or pine straw to conserve moisture and maintain soil acidity, and irrigate consistently during fruit swell, since rabbiteye blueberries have shallow, fibrous roots that dry out quickly in Gulf Coast heat.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Rabbiteye Blueberry Varieties
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Blueberry Variety Trials

planting.note: Plant during winter dormancy in very acidic, well-drained soil; Centurion is a very late-ripening, cold-hardy rabbiteye that requires a cross-pollinating companion, since it is not self-fruitful.

directions: Amend soil to a strongly acidic pH 4.5–5.0 with peat moss or sulfur before planting; Centurion is a USDA-ARS-released rabbiteye blueberry prized as one of the latest-ripening varieties available, extending the harvest well past Tifblue into late July and into August in zone 8–9 and stretching the fresh-picking season for home growers and u-pick operations alike. It is also among the more cold-hardy rabbiteye selections, tolerating winter temperatures further north than many older varieties. Berries are small to medium, dark blue, firm, and flavorful, holding well on the bush without softening even in late-season heat. Plant with an early- or midseason variety such as Climax or Brightwell for cross-pollination, since rabbiteye blueberries including Centurion set little fruit without a compatible partner nearby. Established Centurion bushes are vigorous and heavy-bearing; renew a portion of the oldest canes each winter by cutting them to the ground to keep the bush productive and to encourage fresh, high-yielding new wood.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — Small Fruit Cultivar Releases
University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Rabbiteye Blueberry Varieties
North Carolina State Extension — Blueberry Cultivar Evaluations
